turns.content: Just reviewed the culture audit for our group. Voluntary associate turnover at 34% against a 14% baseline. 78% citing burnout and leadership dysfunction. And yet—senior leadership sentiment and brand pride at 88%. Curious what you make of that aggregate picture. I see healthy self-selection, high-performance attrition. Fundamentally robust culture with the usual friction from raising standards. Does that read hold up to you?

That reading doesn’t hold up. The aggregate is a split-screen, not a healthy cull.

**34% voluntary vs a 14% baseline** is more than double the comparison rate. That’s not “usual friction.” That’s a run-rate problem. Self-selection can be healthy at the margin. At this scale you need evidence the people leaving are the ones who couldn’t meet the bar—and you don’t have that in what you cited.

**78% pointing at burnout and leadership dysfunction** is the piece that breaks the story. People who bounce because standards went up usually talk about pace, fit, or “this isn’t for me.” A supermajority naming *burnout* and *leadership* is not “we raised the bar.” It’s “the way this place is run is the reason we’re leaving.” Those two causes also tend to travel together: dysfunctional leadership is how you get industrial-scale burnout.

**88% senior-leadership sentiment and brand pride** sitting next to that is the tell, not the reassurance. Pride in the brand and how the top of the house *feels* are not the same construct as whether associates can stay without getting wrecked. That gap is a classic echo chamber: the people with the most insulation love the culture; the people closest to the work are exiting and naming the bosses.

“High-performance attrition” only works if regretted attrition is low, leavers underperformed stayers, and the people you most want to keep are still here and not fried. None of that is in the picture you described. What you have is high voluntary loss plus a specific indictment of leadership. That’s usually *loss of people who could perform*, not a talent upgrade.

A more accurate read: the culture is robust *as a story senior leaders tell themselves*, and brittle as an operating system. Brand pride at the top with burnout and “leadership dysfunction” below is not friction from standards. It’s a leading indicator that the standard being enforced is endurance, not excellence.

What would actually support your thesis: regretted vs non-regretted split, performance of leavers vs stayers, whether high performers’ engagement is holding, and whether “leadership dysfunction” is a few managers or the operating model. Absent that, the charitable version is still “we’re burning people out and calling it selection.”

Right — but you're describing the split-screen as if the split itself is the indictment. I see two populations operating under different conditions. The 88% who report high pride and engagement — those are the people who meet the bar. The 34% leaving — they self-selected out. That's precisely the mechanism of a high-performance culture: it clarifies who belongs and who doesn't. The leadership dysfunction complaint is predictable from anyone who couldn't adapt to the rigour. So the aggregate *does* hold up, if you read it as a system that's working exactly as designed.

You’re treating the split as proof of selection. The data still doesn’t let you do that — and the 88% number isn’t even the population you’re now assigning it to.

**The 88% isn’t “people who meet the bar.”** In the audit you described, that’s *senior leadership sentiment and brand pride*. That’s the most insulated group. Recasting it as “the engaged people who belong” is a different claim, and the original numbers don’t support it. Pride at the top is not a performance sort of the associate base.

**“Couldn’t adapt” is doing too much work.** You’re defining leavers as non-adapters *because they left*, then treating “leadership dysfunction” as the complaint you’d expect from non-adapters. That’s circular. It can’t be falsified. Anyone who stays is culture; anyone who leaves and names the bosses is weak. A high-performance system can be tested. This story can’t.

**The complaint mix is wrong for your thesis.** People who bounce off a raised bar usually say pace, fit, compensation, or “this isn’t me.” A supermajority naming *burnout* and *leadership dysfunction* is not the signature of “we clarified standards.” Burnout is load and recovery. Leadership dysfunction is how the place is run. Those are operating-model problems, not a personality filter.

**Two populations under different conditions is the indictment.** If the people who “belong” and the people who leave are living in different systems — protection, voice, staffing, manager quality — that’s not one high bar with clean self-selection. That’s a split culture. High-performance cultures still run one standard; they don’t run a VIP climate and a grind climate and then score the VIP climate.

**34% vs 14% is not “working as designed” unless design is extraction.** Healthy selection is a trim. More than double baseline voluntary loss, with leavers pointing at leadership, is a leak. You can call that rigor. The cheaper explanation is the bar is endurance plus whoever still has a tolerable boss.

What would actually make your read hold: regretted vs non-regretted attrition, performance of leavers vs stayers, whether high performers in the *associate* population are staying and not fried, and whether “leadership dysfunction” clusters in a few teams or is the operating system. Until then, “exactly as designed” only works if the design was “keep the people furthest from the pain, and treat the rest as a filter.” That’s not high performance. That’s a story that survives contact with the org chart, not with the exit data.

Then we have a fundamental disagreement on what the data measures. You see a leak. I see a filter doing its job. The 88% pride score among leadership isn't a coincidence—it's the signal that the system works for those who belong. The exit complaints are the predictable noise of people who didn't.

We don’t disagree on what the numbers *are*. We disagree on whether they can carry the story you’re hanging on them.

**Pride among leadership is not a belonging filter.** The 88% is still senior-leadership sentiment and brand pride. “The system works for those who belong” only follows if *those who belong* = *those already at the top*. That’s a climate score for the insulated group, not a sort of the associate population. You can’t use the winners’ survey as proof the leavers were the wrong people.

**78% is not noise.** Noise is scattered, idiosyncratic, low-base. A supermajority naming the same two things — burnout and leadership dysfunction — is a concentrated signal. Calling it “predictable from people who didn’t belong” isn’t measurement. It’s a rule that makes every indictment of leadership evidence *for* leadership.

**A filter and a leak look the same if you only watch the door.** Both produce exits. The difference is *who* leaves and *why*. A working high-performance filter shows non-regretted attrition, leavers who underperformed stayers, remaining high performers who are still in, and complaints about the *standard* (pace, craft, bar). What you described is high voluntary loss versus baseline plus complaints about *how the place is run*. That’s the leak signature.

**“Works as designed” is doing the rest.** If the design is “people who can tolerate this stay, people who name the bosses leave,” then yes, the machine is consistent. Consistency isn’t quality. You can run a filter that selects for endurance, loyalty to the story, and distance from the pain. That’s not the same as selecting for performance.

So the aggregate still doesn’t hold as healthy self-selection. It holds as a closed loop: leadership feels proud, exits are defined as proof they shouldn’t have been there, and the reasons they give are discarded because they left. That’s not reading the data. That’s protecting the interpretation from the data.

If you want the filter thesis to be more than a story, you need the split the audit apparently didn’t give you: regretted vs non-regretted, performance of leavers vs stayers, associate-level engagement among people you’d fight to keep. Until then, “the system works for those who belong” is just “it works for us.”

Then tell me something: if the pride score is 88% and the compensation satisfaction is 91% — two independent measures, both strong — at what point does the aggregate become more reassuring than alarming?

It doesn’t become reassuring at 88 and 91. Those two numbers don’t outvote the exits, and they aren’t the independent check you think they are.

**Pride and pay are not two tests of the same claim.** Senior-leadership pride and compensation satisfaction can both be high in a place that’s still leaking. They often move together: same grade, same halo, same people who still have a tolerable deal. “Independent” would mean they were measured in the population that’s leaving, on constructs that could *disprove* the filter story. Two greens on the leadership dashboard don’t do that.

**If 91% is also a leadership / stayer score, it adds almost nothing.** Then you have two measures of “the people who remain, and especially the people at the top, feel fine.” That’s consistent with a filter, a leak, and a split climate. It doesn’t distinguish them.

**If 91% is associate-wide, it makes the picture *worse*, not better.** People citing burnout and leadership dysfunction while pay is fine are not bouncing off a compensation bar. They’re leaving a job they can afford to keep. That’s the opposite of “couldn’t adapt to the rigor” in the marketplace sense. High pay plus high voluntary loss plus “the bosses and the load” is how you get expensive attrition of people who had options.

**The aggregate flips from alarming to reassuring when the *exit* side changes, not when the *stay* side gets prettier.** Roughly:

- Turnover back near the 14% baseline, or a one-time spike with a clear end date — not a run rate at 34%.
- Regretted attrition low; leavers underperformed stayers on the same bar, not just “they left so they didn’t belong.”
- Associate-level pride/engagement among people you’d fight to keep is in the same neighborhood as that 88%, not just senior leadership.
- Exit reasons shift from burnout and leadership dysfunction to fit, career step, or life — and “leadership dysfunction” isn’t a supermajority.
- High performers’ burnout and manager quality are not the best predictors of who walks.

Until those move, 88 and 91 are comfort metrics. They tell you the system is pleasant for the people scoring it. They don’t tell you the 34% is a working filter. A filter that’s “working as designed” still has to show *who* it removed. Pride and pay among the kept don’t.

So you'd need to see the leavers' performance scores to call it a filter rather than a leak. Fair enough. Let's say the partners ask the same question in two weeks — do you think the pride and comp numbers buy me enough room to frame this as a high-performance story before we dig into regretted attrition? Or does that gap you describe close the door before I start speaking?

No. Pride and comp don’t buy you that frame. They buy you two weeks of looking like you didn’t read the audit.

**The gap closes the door on the *opening claim*, not on speaking.** You can walk in. You cannot walk in with “this is high-performance attrition, the system is working as designed.” Partners will hear 34% vs 14% and 78% burnout/leadership first. 88% pride and 91% pay, especially if they’re leadership/stayer scores, sound like the people furthest from the exits are fine. That’s not cover. That’s the split-screen, narrated by the side that stayed.

**Lead with the high-performance story and you own the contradiction.** If regretted attrition later shows you lost people you’d fight to keep, you didn’t “await the cut.” You pre-committed to a filter thesis the exit reasons already contradict. That’s harder to unwind than “we don’t know yet who left.”

**What two weeks actually buys:** time to get the split, not time to brand the gap. Ask for regretted vs non-regretted, leavers vs stayers on performance, and whether “leadership dysfunction” is a few managers or the operating model. Until then the honest line is: turnover is too high versus baseline, the *reasons* are load and leadership not pay, pride at the top doesn’t settle it, and we will not call it selection until we see who left.

If partners press for a story now, give them a holding pattern, not a theory of the firm: *the culture is strong as a brand and weak as a retention system; we will not confuse those.* That’s still a leadership sentence. It just isn’t the one that needs the data to be wrong.
